concepts.title: Index of Refraction
concepts.one_liner: The index of refraction $n$ of a medium is a value inversely proportional to both the wavelength and the speed of light within that medium.
concepts.content: Both the wavelength and the speed of light in a medium are inversely proportional to the index of refraction of that medium, denoted as $n$. The $n$ for a vacuum is 1.
concepts.motivation_md: The index of refraction is a fundamental property of materials that determines how much light will bend (refract) and slow down when entering the medium, which is essential for designing lenses.
concepts.recap_md:
- The index of refraction $n$ is inversely proportional to the speed of light in a medium.
- The index of refraction for a vacuum is defined as 1.

- The index of refraction for a vacuum is defined as 1.

concepts.title: Lens
concepts.one_liner: A lens is a transparent material shaped to focus light from a surface point onto a common position on a sensor.
concepts.content: A lens is a specially shaped piece of transparent material, positioned to focus light from a surface point onto a sensor. In an ideal world, a lens focusing light from a surface onto a sensor plane has the property that every light ray from the surface point that passes through the lens is refracted onto a common position at the sensor, no matter what part of the lens the ray from the surface hits. This dramatically increases the light-gathering ability of the camera system, overcoming the poor light-gathering properties of a pinhole camera system.
concepts.motivation_md: Lenses solve the light-gathering limitations of pinhole cameras by allowing many rays from a single point to be collected and focused back to a single point, creating a brighter image.
concepts.recap_md:
- A lens uses refraction to focus light rays from a single point to a common position.
- Lenses significantly improve the light-gathering ability of imaging systems compared to pinholes.

concepts.title: Small Angle Approximation of Snell's Law
concepts.one_liner: For small angles in radians, Snell's law simplifies to $\theta_1 = n \theta_2$ when assuming the index of refraction of air is 1.
concepts.content: For small angles $\theta$ denoted in radians, $\sin(\theta) \approx \theta$. If we also assume the index of refraction of air is 1 (it is 1.0003) and denote the index of refraction of lens glass as $n$, then Snell's law becomes $$\theta_1 = n \theta_2,$$ for small bending angles $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$.
concepts.motivation_md: This approximation simplifies the complex trigonometric calculations of refraction into linear relationships, making it much easier to derive formulas for lens design.
concepts.recap_md:
- Uses the approximation $\sin(\theta) \approx \theta$ for small angles in radians.
- Simplifies Snell's law to $\theta_1 = n \theta_2$ for air-to-glass interfaces.

concepts.title: Lens Surface Angle Derivation
concepts.one_liner: The lens surface angle $\theta_S$ must be linearly proportional to the distance from the optical axis to ensure rays from a point focus correctly.
concepts.content:
Consider a lens and two points along its optical axis at a distance $a$ and $b$ from the lens. We seek to find a surface shape for a lens which creates the light paths shown in (Figure a): light leaving from any direction at point $a$ will be focused to arrive at point $b$. (Figure b) shows a view of (Figure a), with angles and distances distorted for clarity of labeling.

(see figure: A diagram of a thin lens on a horizontal optical axis. A blue light ray originates from a point on the axis at distance $a$ to the left of the lens, making an angle $\theta_1$ with the axis. The ray...)

(see figure: A ray diagram of a thin lens showing a light ray originating from a point at distance $a$ on the optical axis, refracting through two curved surfaces, and converging at a point at distance $b$. The...)

We make use of several approximations that commonly hold for imaging systems: the deviations in angle from the optical axes are very small (the paraxial approximation) and the lens is modeled to have negligible thickness compared with other distances along the optical axis (the thin lens approximation). Under those approximations, we can write simple expressions for the bending angles shown in (Figure b) as a function of $\theta_S$, the lens surface orientation at height $c$. These relations are summarized below:

- Initial angle: $\theta_1 = c/a$ (Small angle approx.)
- Front surface refraction: $n \theta_2 = \theta_1 + \theta_S$ (Snell's law, small angle approx.)
- Internal ray relation: $2 \theta_S = \theta_2 + \theta_3$ (Symmetry of lens, thin lens approx.)
- Back surface refraction: $n \theta_3 = \theta_4 + \theta_S$ (Snell's law, small angle approx.)
- Final angle: $\theta_4 = c/b$ (Small angle approx.)

By algebraically eliminating the angles $\theta_1$ through $\theta_4$, we find the condition on the lens surface angle, $\theta_S$, as a function of the distance $c$ from the optical axis:
$$\theta_S = \frac{c}{2(n-1)} \left( \frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{b} \right)$$

This relationship creates the effect that every ray emanating at a small angle from point $a$ will be focused to point $b$. The result shows that the lens surface angle, $\theta_S$, must deviate from flat in linear proportion to the distance $c$ from the center of the lens.
concepts.motivation_md: This derivation determines the specific geometric shape a lens surface must have to perfectly focus light from a specific object distance to a specific image distance.
concepts.recap_md:
- Relates the surface angle $\theta_S$ to the object distance $a$, image distance $b$, and height $c$.
- Shows that for ideal focusing, the surface angle must be linearly proportional to the distance from the optical axis.

concepts.title: Paraxial Approximation
concepts.one_liner: The paraxial approximation assumes that the deviations in angle from the optical axis are very small.
concepts.content: The paraxial approximation is an approximation used in imaging systems where the deviations in angle from the optical axes are assumed to be very small.
concepts.motivation_md: This approximation allows for the use of small-angle trigonometric simplifications, which makes the mathematics of optical systems linear and solvable.
concepts.recap_md:
- Assumes light rays travel at very small angles relative to the optical axis.
- Enables the use of $\sin(\theta) \approx \theta$ and $\tan(\theta) \approx \theta$.

slots.motivation: This approximation allows for the use of small-angle trigonometric simplifications, which makes the mathematics of optical systems linear and solvable.

concepts.title: Thin Lens Approximation
concepts.one_liner: The thin lens approximation models a lens as having negligible thickness compared to other distances along the optical axis.
concepts.content: In the thin lens approximation, the lens is modeled to have negligible thickness compared with other distances along the optical axis, such as the object and image distances.
concepts.motivation_md: By ignoring the thickness of the lens, we can simplify the refraction calculations by treating the two surfaces of the lens as if they exist at the same plane.
concepts.recap_md:
- Assumes the physical thickness of the lens is small enough to be ignored.
- Simplifies the geometry of light rays passing through the front and back surfaces.

concepts.title: Spherical Lens Surface Property
concepts.one_liner: For small angles, a spherical lens surface satisfies the focusing requirement that the surface angle is proportional to the distance from the axis.
concepts.content: In the thin lens approximation, both parabolic and spherical shapes satisfy the constraint on the lens surface slope required for focusing. For a spherical lens surface curving according to a radius $R$, we have $\sin(\theta_S) = c/R$. For small angles $\theta_S$, this reduces to $$\theta_S = \frac{c}{R},$$ where $R$ is the radius of the sphere. This has the desired property that $\theta_S \propto c$.
concepts.motivation_md: Spherical surfaces are much easier to manufacture than complex parabolic shapes; this property shows that spherical lenses are a valid approximation for focusing light under paraxial conditions.
concepts.recap_md:
- Spherical surfaces satisfy the linear slope requirement $\theta_S \propto c$ for small angles.
- The relationship is given by $\theta_S = c/R$.

slots.motivation: Spherical surfaces are much easier to manufacture than complex parabolic shapes; this property shows that spherical lenses are a valid approximation for focusing light under paraxial conditions.
slots.key_passage:

- The relationship is given by $\theta_S = c/R$.

concepts.title: Lensmaker's Formula
concepts.one_liner: The Lensmaker's Formula relates the object distance, image distance, and focal length of a lens.
concepts.content: Substituting the spherical surface property into the focusing condition yields the Lensmaker's Formula: $$\frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{b} = \frac{1}{f},$$ where the lens focal length, $f$, is defined to be $$f = \frac{R}{2(n-1)}$$.
concepts.motivation_md: This formula is the fundamental tool for determining where an image will be formed based on the physical properties of the lens (radius and refractive index) and the position of the object.
concepts.recap_md:
- Relates object distance $a$ and image distance $b$ to focal length $f$.
- Defines focal length $f$ in terms of the lens radius $R$ and refractive index $n$.

slots.motivation: This formula is the fundamental tool for determining where an image will be formed based on the physical properties of the lens (radius and refractive index) and the position of the object.
slots.key_passage:

- Defines focal length $f$ in terms of the lens radius $R$ and refractive index $n$.

concepts.title: Snell's Law
concepts.one_liner: Snell's Law relates the bending angles of refraction to the indices of refraction at a material interface.
concepts.content:
At a material boundary, Snell's Law relates the bending angles of refraction, $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$, to the indices of refraction, $n_1$ and $n_2$, of the materials. Both the wavelength and the speed of light in a medium are inversely proportional to the index of refraction $n$. The $n$ for a vacuum is 1. For the geometry illustrated in @fig-snell, we have:

$$n_1 \sin(\theta_1) = n_2 \sin(\theta_2)$$

where $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$ are the angles with respect to the surface normal of the incident and outgoing light rays. Snell's law can be derived by matching the wavelength of light projected along the material interface boundary across each side of the boundary.

(see figure: A diagram illustrating Snell's Law of refraction at a horizontal interface between two media with refractive indices $n_1$ and $n_2$. A light ray travels from the top medium ($n_1$) into the bottom...)

(see figure: A photograph of a straight black rod partially submerged in water, demonstrating the effect of refraction. The rod appears to bend sharply at the water's surface, making the submerged portion look...)
concepts.motivation_md: Snell's Law is fundamental for understanding how light behaves when passing through different media, which is essential for designing lenses and understanding image formation in computer vision.

concepts.title: Focal Plane
concepts.one_liner: The focal plane is a plane outside a camera that is conjugate to the sensor plane, such that objects within it are focused sharply.
concepts.content: Assume that a lens is part of a camera, focusing light from the world onto the camera's sensor. If a plane outside of the camera, called the focal plane, and the camera's sensor plane are at conjugate positions, then an object in the focal plane is focused sharply onto the sensor plane. All rays from a point on the object's surface will come into focus at a point in the sensor plane.
concepts.motivation_md: To understand how a camera captures sharp images, we must identify the specific plane in space where objects are perfectly mapped to points on the sensor.

concepts.title: Depth of Field Derivation
concepts.one_liner: The depth of field $D$ can be derived from geometric considerations and is approximately $2 N C U^2 / f^2$ when the circle of confusion is small.
concepts.content:
(see figure: Circle of confusion and depth of field. (Top) Variables used in the computation of the depth of field of a lens. (Bottom) The elongation of the depth of field size for a given tolerable circle of confusion results from narrowing the lens aperture @Levoy2010. The catch is that narrowing the aperture results in less light reaching the sensor plane.)

We can calculate the depth of field from geometric considerations. A camera's f-number, written $N$, is the ratio of the focal length of the lens divided by the diameter of the lens aperture, $A$: $N = f/A$. Let the diameter of the circle of confusion be $C$. If the distance $U$ of the focal plane to the camera is much larger than the focal length ($U >> f$), then the diameter of the focal plane imaged onto the circle of confusion is approximately $C U/f$. By similar triangles, we have:

$$\frac{D_1 f}{C U} = \frac{U - D_1}{\frac{f}{N}}$$

Also by similar triangles, we have:

$$\frac{D_2 f}{C U} = \frac{D_2+U}{\frac{f}{N}}$$

Defining the depth of field $D$ to be $D = D_1 + D_2$, and combining terms, we have:

$$D = \frac{2 N C U^2 f^2}{f^4 - N^2 C^2 U^2}$$

When the circle of confusion $C$ is much smaller than the lens aperture $f/N$, the term $N^2 C^2 D^2$ can be ignored relative to $f^4$, yielding the approximation:

$$D \approx \frac{2 N C U^2}{f^2}$$

Note that for smaller camera f-numbers $N$ (larger apertures), the depth of field decreases in proportion.
concepts.motivation_md: Deriving the depth of field formula allows photographers and engineers to quantify how aperture, focal length, and distance affect the range of sharp focus in an image.

concepts.title: Depth of Field
concepts.one_liner: Depth of field is the region around the plane of focus where the resulting blur at the sensor plane is within a tolerable limit.
concepts.content: The region around the plane of focus that results in a blur at the sensor plane that is smaller than some tolerance is called the depth of field.
concepts.motivation_md: In photography and vision, it is rarely possible to have everything in focus; depth of field defines the acceptable range of sharpness for a given setup.

concepts.title: f-number
concepts.one_liner: The f-number $N$ is the ratio of a lens's focal length to its aperture diameter.
concepts.content: A camera's f-number, written $N$, is the ratio of the focal length of the lens divided by the diameter of the lens that light passes through, called the aperture, $A$: $N = f/A$.
concepts.motivation_md: The f-number provides a standardized way to describe the light-gathering ability and depth of field characteristics of a lens, regardless of its absolute size.

concepts.title: Aperture
concepts.one_liner: The aperture is the diameter of the lens through which light passes.
concepts.content: The aperture, $A$, is the diameter of the lens that light passes through. It is related to the f-number $N$ and focal length $f$ by the equation $N = f/A$.
concepts.motivation_md: Aperture controls the amount of light entering the camera and significantly influences the depth of field.
concepts.recap_md: [ "- Aperture $A$ is the physical diameter of the lens opening.", "- It is a primary factor in determining the f-number and exposure." ]

concepts.title: Concave Lens
concepts.one_liner: A concave lens has surfaces that bow inward, causing parallel rays to diverge and appear to emanate from a virtual focus.
concepts.content:
Concave lenses have a lens surface curve bowing inward toward the center of the lens. Parallel rays entering a concave lens will be bent away from the lens center by the same amount they would be bent toward the center axis for a convex lens of the same radii of curvature. This leads to a concave lens bringing parallel rays to a virtual focus, a point from which the diverging rays leaving the lens appear to be emanating. This is illustrated in (see figure: A ray diagram showing parallel light rays entering a concave lens from the left. The rays diverge as they exit the lens to the right, and dashed lines trace their paths backward to a single virtual...) on-axis, and (see figure: A ray diagram showing parallel light rays entering a concave lens from the left at a downward angle. The rays diverge upon exiting the lens, and dashed lines trace their paths backward to a single...) for off-axis parallel rays.

(see figure: A diagram of a convex lens showing three parallel horizontal rays entering from the left. The rays are refracted as they pass through the lens, converging at a single focal point marked by a blue dot...)

The mathematics of the ray bending is similar to that for convex lenses, except the focal length of concave lenses has a negative value. The focus point for a set of parallel rays entering a concave lens from the left is also on the left side of the lens. It is a virtual focal point, and from the right side of the lens, the emanating rays appear to be originating from the point at distance $-f$ to the left of the lens.
concepts.motivation_md: Concave lenses are essential for diverging light, correcting vision (nearsightedness), and constructing complex optical systems like telescopes.
concepts.recap_md: [ "- Concave lenses bow inward and cause light rays to diverge.", "- They possess a negative focal length.", "- Parallel rays appear to originate from a virtual focal point on the same side as the source." ]

The rays diverge as they exit the lens to the right, and dashed lines trace their paths backward to a single virtual...) on-axis, and (see figure: A ray diagram showing parallel light rays entering a concave lens from the left at a downward angle. The rays diverge upon exiting the lens, and dashed lines trace their paths backward to a single...) for off-axis parallel rays.

(see figure: A diagram of a convex lens showing three parallel horizontal rays entering from the left. The rays are refracted as they pass through the lens, converging at a single focal point marked by a blue dot...)

The mathematics of the ray bending is similar to that for convex lenses, except the focal length of concave lenses has a negative value. The focus point for a set of parallel rays entering a concave lens from the left is also on the left side of the lens. It is a virtual focal point, and from the right side of the lens, the emanating rays appear to be originating from the point at distance $-f$ to the left of the lens.

concepts.title: Telescope Magnification
concepts.one_liner: Telescope magnification $M$ is the ratio of the angular deviation of an output ray to that of an input ray, given by $M = f_1/f_2$.
concepts.content:
The properties of convex and concave lenses can be used to make a telescope. As shown in (see figure: A ray diagram of a Galilean telescope consisting of two lenses. Parallel rays from the left pass through a convex lens (lens 1) and converge toward its focal point at distance $f_1$. Before reaching...), we position a convex lens (lens 1) with a long focal length $f_1$ and a concave lens (lens 2) with a shorter focal length $f_2$ such that each are $f_1$ and $f_2$ away from a common point. This configuration causes parallel rays from a distant object to become a compressed set of parallel rays leaving lens 2. 

(see figure: A ray diagram of a Galilean telescope featuring a convex lens (lens 1) and a concave lens (lens 2) aligned on a horizontal optical axis. Parallel rays enter lens 1 from the left at a small angle...)

The magnification of the telescope is the ratio $M$ of the angular deviation of an output ray, $\delta_o$, to the angular deviation of an input ray, $\delta_i$. Using the small angle approximation, we have $\delta_i f_1 = d$ and $\delta_o f_2 = d$, where $d$ is the focal point offset. Substituting for $d$ gives:

$$M = \frac{\delta_o}{\delta_i} = \frac{f_1}{f_2}$$

where $M$ is the amplification of the parallel ray bending angles.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding telescope magnification allows us to design optical instruments that make distant objects appear larger by increasing the angle at which light enters the eye.

concepts.title: Focal Length
concepts.one_liner: The focal length $f$ of a lens is defined by the relationship $f = \frac{R}{2(n-1)}$.
concepts.content:
The lens focal length, $f$, is defined to be 

$$f = \frac{R}{2(n-1)}$$

where $R$ is the radius of curvature and $n$ is the refractive index.
concepts.motivation_md: Focal length is a fundamental property of a lens that determines its ability to converge or diverge light, serving as a key parameter in the lensmaker's equation.

concepts.title: Off-Axis Focusing
concepts.one_liner: Under paraxial and thin lens approximations, the lensmaker's equation remains valid for light originating from points off the optical axis.
concepts.content:
The lensmaker's equation also holds for light originating off the optical axis. This can be shown by rotating the lens through an angle $\theta_R$ in the derivation, effectively adding $\theta_R$ to $\theta_S$. Consequently, under the paraxial and thin lens approximations, the lens focuses light from points on a plane onto points on a second plane, where both planes are perpendicular to the optical axis.

![Considering light from off-axis sources is equivalent to rotating the lens surface by $\theta_R$, for small angles $\theta_R$. The lens focuses rays from off-axis points like $P_1$, as well as from the on-axis point, $P_0$.](figures/imaging/offAxis.png){#fig-rotatedLens width="100%"}

concepts.title: Generalized Lensmaker's Formula
concepts.one_liner: The generalized lensmaker's formula accounts for lenses with different radii of curvature on their front and back faces.
concepts.content:
The lensmaker's equation can be generalized for the case of a lens with different radii of curvature, $R_1$ and $R_2$, on the front and back faces. By defining the left and right surface angles $\theta_{s_1}$ and $\theta_{s_2}$, the relationship becomes $\theta_{s_1} + 	heta_{s_2} = 	heta_2 + 	heta_3$. Combined with the substitution $\theta_{S_i} = c / R_i$ for $i = 1$ and $2$, this leads to the generalized formula:

$$\frac{1}{f} = (n-1) \left( \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} \right)$$
concepts.motivation_md: Most real-world lenses are not perfectly symmetrical; this formula allows for the calculation of focal length for lenses with arbitrary curvatures on either side.

concepts.title: Lenses and Perspective Projection
concepts.one_liner: A convex thin lens creates a perspective projection because light passing through its center proceeds without bending, similar to a pinhole camera.
concepts.content:
Using the lensmaker's formula and observations of thin lenses, we can analyze how rays travel in the approximation of geometrical optics. Light passing through the center of a thin lens, where the front and back surfaces are parallel, proceeds without bending. Thus, a convex thin lens images as a pinhole camera does, creating a perspective projection.

concepts.title: Conjugate Points
concepts.one_liner: Conjugate points are two points on opposite sides of a lens such that light from one focuses perfectly onto the other.
concepts.content:
Two points on opposite sides of the lens at distances $a$ and $b$ from the lens that satisfy the lensmaker's equation are known as conjugate points. Light from one conjugate point, traveling through the lens, focuses to the other conjugate point, and vice versa. 

One fundamental property of these points is that every ray passing through one conjugate point and passing through the lens then passes through the other conjugate point. This is the fundamental focusing property of a lens.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding conjugate points is essential for determining where an object must be placed to create a sharp image at a specific sensor location.
concepts.recap_md: - Conjugate points satisfy the lensmaker's equation at distances $a$ and $b$.

concepts.title: Ray Tracing Rules for Thin Lenses
concepts.one_liner: Ray tracing for thin lenses follows specific rules regarding conjugate points, parallel rays, and center-passing rays to determine light paths.
concepts.content:
The rules for tracing light travel through a lens include the following:

1. Every ray passing through one conjugate point and passing through the lens then passes through the conjugate point. This is the fundamental focusing property of a lens.
2. Parallel rays entering the lens all focus to a point at distance $f$ behind the lens. In this case, one of the focal points is at infinity.
3. Any ray passing through the center of the thin lens proceeds in a straight line, as if through a pinhole at the center of the lens. Thus, lenses, like pinholes, render the world in *perspective projection*.
4. Because focused rays render positions onto a plane as does a line passing through the center of the lens, then the magnification of a lens is simply $a/b$, where $a$ is the distance of an in-focus object to the lens, and $b$ is the distance from the lens to a sensor plane.

(see figure: A diagram of a thin convex lens with a horizontal optical axis. Light rays from a single point on the left converge at a single point on the right after passing through the lens. Two blue dots on the...)

(see figure: A ray diagram showing a biconvex lens with light rays originating from the left focal point. Three rays diverge from the focal point, pass through the lens, and emerge on the right side as parallel...)

concepts.title: Lens Magnification
concepts.one_liner: The magnification of a lens is defined as the ratio $a/b$, where $a$ is the object distance and $b$ is the sensor distance.
concepts.content: Because focused rays render positions onto a plane as does a line passing through the center of the lens, then the **magnification** of a lens is simply $a/b$, where $a$ is the distance of an in-focus object to the lens, and $b$ is the distance from the lens to a sensor plane.

concepts.title: Circle of Confusion
concepts.one_liner: A circle of confusion is the blur circle formed on a sensor plane when an object is not at the exact conjugate position to be in sharp focus.
concepts.content:
If a plane outside of a camera, called the **focal plane**, and the camera's sensor plane are at conjugate positions, then an object in the focal plane is focused sharply onto the sensor plane. All rays from a point on the object's surface will come into focus at a point in the sensor plane. However, objects closer or further from the focal plane will come into focus behind or in front of the sensor plane, respectively. This results in a point in the focal plane being imaged as a **circle of confusion** (a blur circle) at the sensor plane.

![Circle of confusion and depth of field. Referring to @fig-rotatedLens, if the object of interest and the camera's sensor plane are related as conjugate points, that is, with distances $a$ and $b$ from the camera lens respecting the lensmaker's formula (@eq-lensmaker), then the object will form an image in sharp focus in the sensor plane. But objects in front of the plane of focus by $\delta_a$ will, in general, come to focus some distance $\delta_b$ behind the sensor plane @Levoy2010.](figures/imaging/circleOfConfusion.png){#fig-circleOfConfusion width="70%"}
concepts.motivation_md: The circle of confusion is the physical basis for depth of field and blur in photography, defining the limits of what we perceive as 'in focus'.
concepts.recap_md: - Out-of-focus points appear as blur circles called circles of confusion.

concepts.title: Pinhole-Lens Sharpness-Brightness Tradeoff
concepts.one_liner: Pinhole cameras can only increase light intake at the expense of image sharpness, a tradeoff that lenses overcome by focusing rays from a single point to a single sensor position.
concepts.content: Pinhole cameras allow more light to enter the camera aperture only at the expense of image sharpness. Lenses overcome that tradeoff by focusing all the rays passing through the lens from a point on a surface to a single position on the sensor plane, creating an image that is both sharp and bright.
concepts.motivation_md: Pinhole cameras face a fundamental physical limit where a larger aperture increases brightness but blurs the image; lenses are necessary to achieve both high light sensitivity and high resolution.
concepts.recap_md: - Pinhole cameras trade off image sharpness for light intake. - Lenses focus multiple rays from a single scene point onto a single sensor point. - This mechanism allows for images that are simultaneously bright and sharp.
